blocks.text: Lesson 2 gave you hinta, kallis, kohtuullinen — enough to state a price. But half the point of a review is comparing: cheaper than expected, more expensive than the competitor, the best shop in town. This lesson gives you that comparing machinery.

blocks.title: The most satisfying review sentence
blocks.text: 'Cheaper than estimated' might be the single most positive thing a Finnish reviewer can say about a repair shop — trust in the original hinta-arvio (Lesson 2) plus a pleasant surprise. You'll see this exact structure, or something very close to it, repeated across many five-star reviews in this corpus.

blocks.content: To compare, add {-mpi|grammar|comparative suffix|-er/more} to the adjective stem. Halpa (cheap) → {halvempi|grammar|comparative|cheaper}. Kallis (expensive) → {kalliimpi|grammar|comparative|more expensive}. The stem sometimes shifts slightly (halpa → halve-, kallis → kallii-) but the -mpi ending is always the signal you're looking at a comparison.

items.en: The other place was more expensive.
The price was more affordable than I expected.

blocks.text: Piece 2 — Mitä and kuin: both mean 'than'

blocks.content: To finish a comparison, Finnish uses {kuin|grammar|comparison word|than} — the standard, textbook word for 'than'. But in casual speech and in these reviews, you'll often see {mitä|grammar|comparison word, colloquial|than} doing the exact same job instead: halvemmalla mitä arvioitu. Same meaning, more relaxed register — remember mä/sä from way back? Same spirit.

items.fi: Käynnistä selviää edullisemmin {kuin|grammar|comparison word|than} ensin arvioitu.
items.en: The visit turns out more affordable than first estimated.

blocks.text: Piece 3 — Superlative: paras, the best of all

blocks.title: Paras — an irregular superlative worth knowing by heart
blocks.text: The regular superlative ending is {-in|grammar|superlative suffix|-est}: halvin (cheapest), kallein (most expensive). But hyvä (good) doesn't play by the rules — its superlative is the irregular word {paras|grammar|superlative, irregular|best}, not 'hyvin'. You'll see paras korjaamo, 'the best repair shop', used as flat, confident praise.

lines.speaker: A
lines.fi: Oliko tämä korjaamo kalliimpi kuin edellinen?
lines.en: Was this repair shop more expensive than the previous one?

lines.speaker: B
lines.fi: Ei, päinvastoin — auto korjattiin halvemmalla mitä arvioitu.
lines.en: No, the opposite — the car was fixed for less than estimated.

lines.speaker: A
lines.en: Would you recommend it to others, then?

lines.speaker: B
lines.fi: Kyllä. Mielestäni tämä on paras korjaamo täällä.
lines.en: Yes. I think this is the best repair shop around here.

blocks.title: Paul Noble Rule
blocks.text: -mpi means 'more', -in means 'most' — that's the entire system, minus one exception (hyvä → paras). Every adjective you've already learned (hyvä, huono, kallis, halpa, ystävällinen) can take these same two endings. Try building kalliimpi and kalliin yourself before checking — you already have everything you need.

blocks.content: Halvemmalla: HAL-vem-mal-la (double 'm', four syllables — take it slow). Kalliimpi: KAL-liim-pi (the double 'ii' is held long — that length is what marks it as comparative, not just kallis). Paras: PA-ras (short, punchy, stress on PA).

blocks.title: What you now own
items: kuin and its colloquial twin mitä, both meaning 'than'
the superlative -in, plus the one irregular exception: hyvä → paras
you can now say a repair shop was cheaper, more expensive, or the best — not just good or bad
you recognise the register difference between kuin and mitä, formal vs colloquial
